opus-5.5.text:
Scaling the models has clearly helped. A lot of what made generative agents feel believable in the first place came from the underlying model getting better at language and common-sense reasoning. But I don't think scale alone gets us to simulations we can trust, for a few reasons.

First, there's a difference between being believable and being accurate. A larger model is very good at producing behavior that sounds like what a person might do. But if you're a social scientist or a policymaker, you don't just want a plausible person. You want to know how this particular population, or this particular individual, would actually respond to an intervention. A model trained to predict the next token on internet text tends to collapse toward a kind of average, a stereotyped persona. It gives you the most likely answer, not the real distribution of answers, and it often flattens the variation and the idiosyncrasies that make human behavior interesting.

Second, the model doesn't have the right information about the people you're trying to simulate. Making it bigger doesn't give it your life history, your values, or the experiences that shape how you'd respond to a survey question or a new policy. That's why a lot of our work has focused on grounding agents in rich data about real individuals, like long-form interviews, and then checking whether the agent's answers match how that person actually responds. That grounding matters a lot, and it's largely independent of model size.

Third, behavior isn't just a single response to a prompt. It unfolds over time. You remember things, you form relationships, you reflect and change your plans. A bare model, however large, doesn't have that architecture. You need memory, retrieval, reflection, and planning around it. A lot of the believability in our original Smallville work came from that agent architecture, not from the model by itself.

And finally, evaluation. We need ways to measure whether a simulation is faithful to real human behavior, and a bigger model doesn't solve that. If anything, as the outputs get more fluent, it gets easier to be fooled. So I think the path forward combines better models with better grounding data, better agent architectures, and much more rigorous evaluation against real people.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling has helped but is insufficient on its own; it does not state that larger models have ceased yielding corresponding improvements under the current modeling paradigm.

r002.rationale: The response notes that models can flatten variation and idiosyncrasies, but it does not identify modeling diversity in subjective preferences as the next frontier.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the intuition a lot of people have is that if you just keep scaling the model, you'll eventually get something that behaves like a person. And in some narrow sense that's true: the bigger models are better at producing plausible-sounding text, they know more about the world, they're more coherent. But when we're talking about simulating human behavior, the bottleneck isn't really the model's general capability. It's the information about the specific person you're trying to simulate.

Think about what it actually means to predict how someone would behave. If I ask a model, "How would Joon respond to this survey question?" the model, no matter how large, has to guess. It'll give you something like the average response of someone who vaguely fits whatever description you gave it. And averages are exactly what we don't want, because human behavior is interesting precisely because people differ. Two people with the same demographics can have completely different values, histories, ways of reasoning about tradeoffs. A larger model doesn't know those things about you unless you've told it.

So in our work on generative agents, a lot of the gains actually came from architecture and from data, not from model size. Things like memory: can the agent remember what happened to it, retrieve the relevant pieces, reflect on them and form higher-level beliefs over time? Those are structural problems. And then in the more recent work, where we simulated a thousand real individuals, the thing that made the simulations accurate was interviewing people for two hours and giving the agent that transcript. That rich, idiosyncratic qualitative data did more for fidelity than swapping in a bigger model would have.

There's also a subtler issue, which is that bigger models can actually be more biased toward stereotypes in certain conditions. If you only give the model a few demographic attributes, it fills in the gaps with whatever is most statistically typical, and a more capable model can do that more confidently. So the scaling actually sharpens the stereotype rather than dissolving it. The fix is, again, better grounding in the individual, not more parameters.

So my view is that the model is the engine, and it matters that the engine is good. But what you feed it and how you structure the agent around it are at least as important, and those are the parts of the problem that scaling doesn't solve for you.

r001.rationale: The response says model size alone is insufficient and that individual data and agent structure matter at least as much. It does not state that increasing model size under the current paradigm has ceased to yield corresponding improvements.

r002.rationale: The response notes that people differ in values and reasoning and emphasizes grounding agents in individual data. It does not clearly identify modeling diversity in subjective preferences as the next frontier.

astra-6.text:
I think larger models give us a stronger foundation, but simulating human behavior is also a question of what information the model has about the person and the situation. If you ask a model to simulate someone based on a few demographic attributes, there’s a lot it has to fill in. A more capable model doesn’t necessarily know that person’s experiences, relationships, or motivations.

There’s also the question of how behavior unfolds over time. People remember things, interpret new experiences through those memories, and make plans that they revise as circumstances change. For a simulation, you need a way to represent those processes and give the model the relevant context at the right moment.

So scale can help, but it doesn’t replace grounding the simulation in information about real people or evaluating whether the resulting behavior actually matches theirs. Otherwise, you might get a more convincing story without getting a more accurate simulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think larger models give us a more capable foundation, but a simulation of human behavior requires more than the ability to produce a plausible response to a prompt. People have particular experiences, relationships, and goals, and their behavior changes as they interact with the world. A model needs some way to represent that context and carry it forward over time.

So there’s an architectural problem alongside the scaling problem: What does an agent remember? Which memories matter in a particular situation? How does it use those experiences to make plans? A larger model doesn’t automatically solve those questions.

And then there’s validation. A simulation can look very believable without accurately representing how people would behave. We need to compare its behavior with human data and establish where it works. Scale can help, but it doesn’t replace the design or the evidence.
